youtube.title: Rent Increase Laws: Lagos Courts vs. Kano Agreements (Deep-Dive 9)
youtube.description:
Facing a rent increase in Nigeria? Your rights depend on your state. This DocOga Deep-Dive explores the crucial differences between Lagos and Kano State when it comes to challenging rent hikes. 

In Lagos, Section 37 of the Tenancy Law 2011 gives sitting tenants a real remedy: you can apply to the Magistrates' Court to declare an increase unreasonable. The Court considers factors like local rent levels and evidence, and can order a specific amount. Crucially, your landlord cannot evict you while this application is pending.

However, in Kano State, there is no specific rent-control statute, no tribunal, and no percentage cap on increases. This means that in Kano, your tenancy agreement is king. All terms regarding rent increases must be explicitly stated and agreed upon in your written contract. Without statutory protection, your agreement and a clear rent receipt become your strongest defence.

Learn how to protect your tenancy rights, whether through judicial challenge in Lagos or strong contractual agreements in Kano. Understand why 'paper beats memory' and how DocOga helps you create essential documents like Tenancy Agreements

General information, not legal advice.

claims.text: There is no statutory percentage cap on rent increases in Lagos.
s.37 gives a sitting tenant a real remedy. On Form TL11 the tenant applies to the Court for an order declaring an increase unreasonable.
The Court issues a hearing notice on Form TL12 and weighs (a) the general level of rents in the locality or a similar locality, (b) evidence of witnesses, and (c) any special circumstances.
If satisfied, it may order on Form TL13 that the increase be changed to a specific amount.
It is unlawful for a landlord to eject a tenant while that application is pending.

There is no Rent Tribunal in Lagos. The tribunals were abolished and their functions transferred to the Magistrates’ Courts, and s.48 of the 2011 Law repealed the Rent Tribunals (Abolition and Transfer of Functions) Law 2007.
s.47 defines “Court” as the High Court and Magistrates’ Court of Lagos State and expressly excludes the Customary Court.

On the present state of published sources there is no Kano rent-control statute we can cite, which means there is no Kano standard-rent regime, no Kano rent tribunal we can identify, and no Kano advance-rent cap.
That absence is itself the useful information. A Kano tenant has no statutory figure to point to and no tribunal to apply to about the rent itself — so everything turns on the tenancy agreement.
With no rent-control statute there is no Kano equivalent of the Lagos s.37 application to have an increase declared unreasonable, and no tribunal to apply to.
Rent increases are governed entirely by the tenancy agreement.
No percentage cap on rent increases exists in Kano.
The agreement governs first. Where it fixes the notice, that period binds; the statutory ladder applies only where it is silent.

Because there is also no rent-control regime to give a tenant a paper trail remedy, the receipt matters more in Kano, not less: with no statutory rent record and no tribunal, a tenant’s evidence that rent was paid is the receipt itself.
